question.prompt: For a finite sequence \(A=(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n)\) of numbers, the Cesàro sum of \(A\) is defined to be \[ \frac{S_1+S_2+\cdots+S_n}{n}, \] where \[ \begin{aligned} S_k&=a_1+a_2+a_3+\cdots+a_k\\ &\qquad(1\le k\le n). \end{aligned} \] If the Cesàro sum of the \(99\)-term sequence \((a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{99})\) is \(1000,\) what is the Cesàro sum of the \(100\)-term sequence \((1,a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{99})?\)

solutions.explanation:
Prepending \(1\) adds \(1\) to every old partial sum and also creates a new first partial sum equal to \(1\). This lets us use the given average without finding any individual \(a_k\).

Because the original \(99\) partial sums have average \(1000\),
\[
S_1+S_2+\cdots+S_{99}=99\cdot1000=99000.
\]
The new sequence has the \(100\) partial sums
\[
1,\quad 1+S_1,\quad 1+S_2,\quad\ldots,\quad 1+S_{99}.
\]
Their total is \(99000+100=99100\). Therefore the new Cesàro sum is
\[
\frac{99100}{100}=\boxed{991},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutions.title: Track the partial sums
